transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just can't seem to get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. It really bothers me. Whenever I have to do business in town, I feel like every banker or county person is just staring right at the cracks and the spots and the sagging skin. My wife tells me I'm making a big deal out of nothing, that I just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life. But I just can't seem to let it go.

When you're thinking about how your face and hands look, do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like picking at your skin, examining yourself in mirrors, or comparing how you look to other people?

Well, yeah, I do. Especially before I have to leave the farm for something important, like a loan meeting at the bank or setting up a table at the craft fair. I'll catch myself checking the bathroom mirror, and then I'll do it again in the truck mirror. I'll just sit there, turning my hat this way and that, trying to see if it casts a shadow to hide the wrinkles. And I definitely compare myself. I'll look at my hands and then think about the younger hands of the guys we hire on, or the folks in town. Sometimes I get so caught up doing all this that I end up wasting time I really should be spending getting work done around the farm.
Beyond the worry about your face and hands, do you find yourself frequently worried or anxious about other things in your life, like your health, finances, or how things are going on the farm?

No, not really. I mean, farming's always a gamble with the weather and prices, so there's the usual stress there. But I wouldn't say I'm worried sick about it or anything. My health is fine, and we make ends meet alright. It's really just... just the way I look that gets to me. That's the only thing that really eats up my thoughts.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F48.1 (neurasthenia) - patient denies generalized worry about health, finances, or other life domains. Ruled out F41.1 (generalized anxiety disorder) - anxiety is circumscribed to appearance only, not pervasive. The repetitive mirror checking, comparison behaviors, significant time spent on appearance concerns, and distress despite reassurance from wife are classic for Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.21).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD). He demonstrates preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (facial wrinkles, age spots, sagging skin on face and hands) that is not observable or appears slight to others. He engages in repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, mirror comparisons, examining appearance in multiple reflective surfaces) in response to the preoccupation. These behaviors consume significant time and cause functional impairment (time wasted that should be spent on farm work). The preoccupation is not better explained by concerns with body fat or weight, and there is no evidence of generalized anxiety or other primary psychiatric disorder. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress and social/occupational impairment.
